title: A proportional-odds violation biases an expected-utility difference in both directions, depending on where the utility increments sit
question: Does a proportional-odds violation bias a target-standardized expected-utility difference in proportion to the utility increments at the violated cut-point, and does relaxing proportional odds remove it?
design: Four-category ordinal outcome with proportional odds or a violation at the bottom or top cut-point; utilities with increments at the bottom or top; proportional-odds and separate cut-point logistic regressions standardized over a shifted target. 3 cells, 400 replicates each.
answer: Not as predicted. A proportional-odds violation biased the target-standardized expected-utility difference whichever end carried the utility increments: by -0.025 and -0.047 with the increments at the violated cut-point and by +0.026 and +0.024 at the other end, with coverage 0.67 to 0.85. The single coefficient understates the effect at the violated cut-point and overstates it elsewhere. Separate cut-point logistic models were unbiased with coverage 0.93 to 0.98 in every cell.
findings: Registered primary (aligned bias at least twice misaligned) not confirmed: misaligned bias was of similar size and opposite sign.
Under proportional odds both models were unbiased with nominal coverage (null control passed).
Relaxing proportional odds cost little precision: RMSE 0.022 to 0.032 versus 0.023 to 0.056.
not_answered: One individual-data trial rather than an ML-NMR network; separate cut-point regressions as the relaxed model; fixed utilities; no dichotomized-publication arm. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Target-standardized expected-utility difference, A minus C
n_sim: 400 per cell, 3 cells, two utility vectors each
